solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Object to play after expertise is seen with poem

indicators.note: after places the play word second, behind the expertise word in the answer

blocks.note: to act is to play a part

explanation.surface: Someone protests at a play's poor craft and verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb of protest, but it is the noun being defined. Kipling's If is the crossword's favourite poem.
explanation.definitionFit: An artifact is a man-made thing, a synonym for an object of human manufacture.

clue.text: Contrary to most, grand dons hating showers?

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so the wearer ends up wrapped inside the garment

blocks.note: someone who hates showers of rain is against the rain
G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: Unusually, distinguished university dons dislike taking showers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' reads as academics but is the verb: the phrase for hating rain wears the G for grand.
explanation.definitionFit: Going against the grain is an idiom for acting contrary to the usual inclination or the majority.

clue.text: Line from song off a record

blocks.note: first meaning: a path or rail line
second meaning: one recording on an album

explanation.surface: A lyric quoted from a song on an album.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a path or railway line and a single piece of music on an album.

clue.text: God, a good walk spoiled around harbours – due to this?

definitions.text: God, a good walk spoiled around harbours – due to this?

indicators.note: turning around means the game's name is read from its end
to harbour is to shelter something within, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: Odin is the chief Norse god

explanation.surface: A round of golf ruined, with the course awash, prompts a curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A good walk spoiled' is the famous quip about golf. The whole clue is also the definition: a waterlogged course is why the game is spoiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Flooding of a course is exactly the kind of inundation that would ruin a round and leave the greens underwater.

clue.text: Bloke entertaining Earl is good value

indicators.note: a host entertaining a guest has them in the house, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for Earl

explanation.surface: A man hosting an aristocrat finds it a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cheap costs little, so it is a bargain or good value for money.

clue.text: I want to be 12 and barrel about around Norfolk town mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the town's name loses its last letter
turned about means the barrel word is read backwards
around places the cask word on both sides of the town

blocks.note: a tun is a large cask
Diss is a market town in Norfolk, England

explanation.surface: Someone longs to be free and roll a barrel round a Norfolk town.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is the answer NAKED, so the definition is a person who wants to be naked.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturist's wish is to go without clothes, so the speaker of the phrase is one who favours nakedness.

clue.text: Cheery Greek character about to obtain lead over European

indicators.note: turned about means the Greek letter is written backwards
obtaining something means taking it in, so the other pieces go inside

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead

explanation.surface: A cheerful Greek gets the lead role ahead of another European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places lead above European in this down entry. 'Lead' is the metal, not a leading role.
explanation.definitionFit: Upbeat is a synonym for optimistic and cheerful.

clue.text: Terribly dull tie is not a good match

indicators.note: something done terribly is botched, so the letters come out in a muddled order

explanation.surface: A boring necktie clashes with the outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'is' does double duty only in the surface; here it is part of the fodder, and the definition stands alone at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-suited describes things or people poorly matched or unsuited to each other.

clue.text: Woman in article took out what happened around 10?

blocks.note: to drop a player is to take them out of a team

explanation.surface: A woman named in a newspaper story was removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is the AHA MOMENT, so the definition is what happens at the instant of realisation.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for finally understanding something, which is what an aha moment is.

clue.text: Bit of seepage with locks under pressure

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a single letter of it, here its opening one

blocks.note: having tresses, or locks of hair

explanation.surface: A leak with locks fitted, all under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests canal gates beside the seepage, but means hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Stressed is a synonym for strained or anxious, as one feels under pressure.

clue.text: A crossword might give you one flipping laugh a minute!

definitions.text: A crossword might give you one

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the laugh is written backwards

explanation.surface: A crossword gives you a darned laugh every minute!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British oath, but turns the laugh round.
explanation.definitionFit: Solving a clue brings that sudden flash of realisation, the moment of insight that a crossword delivers.

clue.text: One of the army brass must advance left in surge?

indicators.note: the letter standing for left must advance, moving forward and so changing the order

blocks.note: a bugle is a brass instrument used by the army

explanation.surface: A senior officer leads an advance on the left flank of a surge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests top officers but is the instrument; the L of the bugle moves forward two places.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulge is a swelling, and also a sudden rise or surge in numbers.

clue.text: Contrary uni boss drinks in King's Head out of habit

indicators.note: going contrary means running the other way, so the boss is read backwards
the head of a word is its first letter
drinking something in takes it inside

blocks.note: a dean heads a university faculty

explanation.surface: A bloody-minded college head drinks at the King's Head pub, out of habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of habit' reads as routine, but a habit is a monk's robe, so out of it one is unclothed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of one's habit, the monastic garment, leaves one without clothes, a cryptic sense of nude.

clue.text: Early Trump era atrocious, distressing essentially

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, here its central letter
something atrocious is a mess, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Political commentary: the early days of a presidency are dreadful and upsetting.
explanation.definitionFit: Premature means happening before the proper time, a synonym for too soon.

clue.text: 10 workers touring large, empty edifices without residents

indicators.note: emptied of its inside, only the outer letters of the buildings word survive
touring means going round, so the workers wrap around the rest

blocks.note: the number written as a word
worker ants: the standard crossword workers

explanation.surface: Ten labourers tour large vacant buildings that have no one living in them.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' is a cross-reference in disguise only on the surface: here it simply stands for the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenants are residents, so a property lacking them is unoccupied.

clue.text: I love travelling on tours to house of ill-repute

indicators.note: letters that are travelling move around and arrive in a new order
to house something is to give it a home inside

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone loves going on tours that call at a brothel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House of ill-repute' is a stock phrase for a brothel; the split puts 'house' into the wordplay and leaves the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Notorious means famous for something bad, that is, having a poor reputation.

clue.text: Genial new nurses beginning to nurture small biases

indicators.note: a new version of the word has its letters rearranged
the beginning of a word is its first letter
to nurse is to hold something close, so it ends up inside

explanation.surface: Friendly new nurses show a slight partiality at the start of their care.
explanation.definitionFit: Leanings are inclinations or tendencies, the mild preferences that are biases.

clue.text: Amaze boss having made latest start on numbers

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
making something the latest one replaces whatever was last before

blocks.note: a boss is a raised stud or knob

explanation.surface: A manager astonishes by making a late opening on the figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' means a stud, as on a shield, not a manager; its last letter is swapped for the N.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun is to astonish or stupefy, a synonym for amaze.

clue.text: Feeling awfully tense holding one set of holy works

indicators.note: done awfully means badly arranged, so the letters are muddled
holding something keeps it inside

explanation.surface: Feeling very anxious while holding a set of scriptures.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentient means able to perceive or feel, an adjective for capacity of sensation.

clue.text: Detest husband, a tyke without any substance

indicators.note: with no substance means hollowed out, leaving only the outer letters

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Loathing a husband, a lightweight rascal.
explanation.walkthrough: A tyke is a cheeky child or a Yorkshireman; here only its shell is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate is to loathe, a direct synonym of detest.

clue.text: Tough as aggressive old goats might be?

definitions.text: as aggressive old goats might be?

blocks.clueFragment: as aggressive old goats might be?
blocks.note: second meaning, playful: rams and billy goats butt with tough skulls

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal reading: goats that butt need solid heads.
explanation.definitionFit: The compound is an idiom for practical and unsentimental, and literally describes a solid skull.

clue.text: Very harsh split ending in divorce

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: to sever is to cut apart

explanation.surface: A bitter separation ends a marriage in divorce.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe means extremely strict or harsh, as in a harsh punishment.

clue.text: Gang up with nerd to hamper one working in Beds?

indicators.note: letters that are stirred up end in a different order
a hamper is a basket, so the letters enclose another

explanation.surface: A gang teams up with a geek to obstruct someone employed in Bedfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Beds is the abbreviation for Bedfordshire, an English county, but here means flower beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardening means tending plants, which is work done in flower beds.

clue.text: Big argument? No good going back over it!

indicators.note: going back means the abbreviation is read in the other direction
going over it means covering it on both sides

blocks.note: NG is short for no good

explanation.surface: A huge quarrel: no point rehashing it!
explanation.definitionFit: Grown means fully developed or large, as in a grown man.

clue.text: Zero-hour contract worker possibly getting old rate

blocks.note: a temp is a temporary worker, often on a zero-hours contract

explanation.surface: A casual worker on a zero-hours contract gets paid at an outdated rate.
explanation.walkthrough: A zero-hours contract is a British employment contract with no guaranteed hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is speed or pace, as rate is in music or activity.

clue.text: Go light

blocks.note: first meaning: to go with, to suit
second meaning: a stick for lighting fire

explanation.walkthrough: Two words read as a command to set off and ignite; each is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for going together well and a noun for a striking stick that gives a light.

clue.text: Fuss about love

explanation.surface: A lot of bother over romance.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to love intensely, a strong synonym.

clue.text: See Spot go for a new treatment in March?

definitions.note: an adverbial gloss on a style of marching; the answer is the step itself

indicators.note: a new treatment reworks the material, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking the dog Spot for a spring grooming treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month, but the capital hides the parade-ground sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The goose-step is a stiff-legged way of marching associated with military parades.

clue.text: Street in poverty built a dwelling out of bits of wood

definitions.text: built a dwelling out of bits of wood

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed within it

explanation.surface: A poor street dweller made a shack from scrap timber.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition describes birds building with twigs, dressed as a tale of urban poverty.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds that nested made a home from twigs, the bits of wood of the definition.

clue.text: Charlie Brown returned blocks that girl had grabbed

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in reverse
to block something is to stand in its way, sitting inside it

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
she'd is short for she had

explanation.surface: Charlie Brown comes back and blocks something a girl had grabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie Brown is the Peanuts character, but here the two words are split. 'Had' is part of the contraction, so the definition is just the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: Snatched means seized quickly, a synonym for grabbed.
